title: The P&I You Remit Is Not the P&I You Collected: Custodial Reconciliation With an AI Servicing Agent
summary: Investor reporting and custodial accounting is the servicing function that never calls the borrower and never makes the pitch deck, and it is where a servicer loses its approval. How an AI agent runs the daily reconciliation Fannie Mae's Servicing Guide requires across P&I and T&I custodial accounts, why the scheduled/scheduled rule forces more accounts than people expect, and the line between reconciling the money and moving it.
body_markdown:
## The Function Nobody Demos


Every servicing pitch is about the borrower-facing channel: the collections call, the loss-mitigation package, the escrow explanation. The function that actually decides whether a servicer keeps its agency approval is the one nobody demos, because it never talks to a borrower. It is investor reporting and custodial accounting, the daily work of proving that the money the servicer collected, the money sitting in the custodial accounts, and the money reported and remitted to the investor all agree. When they stop agreeing and nobody catches it, the result is not a bad customer review. It is a finding, a corrective action plan, and in a bad case a loss of the servicing portfolio.


I build the servicing agents, and custodial reconciliation is the workflow where I am most careful about what the agent is allowed to touch. The reconciliation is pure, high-volume, rules-bound detail work, which is exactly what an agent is good at. Moving money between accounts and remitting to an investor is a controlled action with real finality, which is exactly the kind of thing an agent should prepare and a human should authorize. Getting that line right is the whole design.


## Why There Are More Accounts Than You Think


The custodial structure is not one bank account. Fannie Mae's Servicing Guide, at[A4-1-02, Establishing Custodial Bank Accounts](https://servicing-guide.fanniemae.com/svc/a4-1-02/establishing-custodial-bank-accounts) , requires a separate principal-and-interest custodial account for each remittance type the servicer reports under, and it bars commingling principal and interest with taxes and insurance in the same account at all. Tax-and-insurance escrow can sit in one T&I account across remittance types or in a separate account per type, at the servicer's choice, but P&I and T&I never share an account.


The rule that surprises people is the scheduled/scheduled one. For scheduled/scheduled remittance, where the servicer remits scheduled principal and interest whether or not the borrower actually paid, the guide requires at least two P&I custodial accounts, so that funds for MBS pools are never commingled with funds for portfolio loans. A servicer that thinks it runs one P&I account is usually running several and reconciling them as if they were one, which is how a shortfall in a pool account hides behind a surplus in a portfolio account until an audit pulls them apart. The remittance type also changes what the reconciliation has to prove. Under actual/actual the servicer remits what it collected, so the account should track collections. Under scheduled remittance the servicer advances its own money to cover what borrowers did not pay, so the account balance and the amount remitted deliberately diverge, and the reconciliation has to account for the advance rather than flag it as a break.


There is a timing rule underneath this too. The Servicing Guide's custodial procedures, in[F-1-03](https://servicing-guide.fanniemae.com/svc/f-1-03/establishing-and-implementing-custodial-accounts) , require the borrower's escrow balance to be deposited into the T&I custodial account no later than one business day after the servicer receives Fannie Mae's purchase proceeds on a newly acquired loan. Custodial accounting is a set of clocks as much as a set of balances, and a late deposit is its own exception.


## What the Agent Reconciles, Every Day


The reconciliation the agent runs is a three-way tie-out performed continuously rather than at month-end. One side is the servicing system of record: what each loan was billed, what posted, how it was applied across principal, interest, escrow, and any suspense, and what advances the servicer made. The second side is the custodial bank accounts: the actual cleared balances and transactions in each P&I and T&I account. The third side is the investor reporting: the loan-level activity reported to Fannie Mae and the remittance drafted against it.


The agent's job is to prove those three agree, loan by loan and account by account, and to isolate the ones that do not. A break is any place the three sides disagree: a payment posted in the system of record that has not cleared the custodial account, a borrower payment collected but not yet reported, a remittance drafted that the account cannot cover, an escrow disbursement that left the T&I account without a matching ledger entry. The agent classifies each break by type and likely cause rather than dumping an undifferentiated exception list on an analyst. A timing break, where a payment is in transit and will clear, is not the same problem as a true shortfall, where money that should be in the account is not, and the agent separates them because they go to different people and carry different urgency.


What makes an agent fit this work is that the breaks are the point and the ties are the noise. Most lines reconcile and need no human attention. The value is in finding the handful that do not, explaining them, and doing it the same way every day so a break that appears on day one is caught on day one instead of surfacing in a quarterly review when it has grown three weeks of related errors behind it. A long-horizon agent holds the reconciliation as a standing goal, wakes on each posting and clearing event, and keeps the three sides tied continuously, which turns the month-end scramble into a running state the servicer can see at any moment.


## Why This Is Governed, and What It Is Governed Against


Custodial accounting is not a model making a credit decision, but it is a control the investor and the regulator both examine, so it carries its own governance weight. The custodial requirements are investor rules, and the escrow side touches Regulation X. The escrow funds the agent reconciles are the same funds governed by the annual escrow analysis under[12 CFR 1024.17](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/chapter-X/part-1024/section-1024.17) , which sets the aggregate accounting method, the permitted cushion, and the shortage and surplus handling. A reconciliation agent that does not understand that the T&I account is governed money, held for the borrower and accounted for under a federal rule, would treat a shortage as an accounting break when it is also a borrower obligation with a statutory process. So the agent reconciles the custodial accounts with the Reg X treatment in view, and an escrow break that implies a shortage against the borrower's account routes with that flagged, not just as a ledger difference.


We validate the reconciliation logic the way we validate any component that produces a conclusion a servicer relies on, and we monitor it for the error that costs the most: a break the agent closed as a timing difference that was actually a true shortfall. That is the custodial equivalent of a confident wrong answer, and it is the one the sampling and the human review over the top of the agent are designed to catch. A break miscategorized as benign is worse than a break the agent escalated unnecessarily, so the thresholds favor escalation on anything touching a real shortfall or a late custodial deposit.


## The Line the Agent Does Not Cross


The agent reconciles. It does not move money and it does not remit on its own. Drafting the remittance, moving funds between custodial accounts, and authorizing the transfer to the investor are controlled actions with finality, and finality is the property that keeps them on the human side of the line. The agent prepares the remittance, proves the account can fund it, attaches the reconciliation that supports it, and presents it for authorization. A person with the authority approves the transfer. The agent executes nothing irreversible that it proposed.


It also stops on the breaks that need judgment rather than research. A true shortfall of any size, a custodial balance that cannot cover a scheduled remittance, a pattern of breaks concentrated in one pool or one investor, an escrow difference that implies a Reg X shortage: these route to the servicing-accounting owner with the break explained and the supporting entries attached. The agent's job on a hard break is to make the human's investigation fast, with the three sides already lined up and the discrepancy isolated, not to resolve it alone.


What the agent takes off the analyst's desk is the daily tie-out across every loan and every account, the classification of thousands of lines into the few that need a person, and the continuous proof that the money agrees. What it leaves is the authorization of the money movement and the judgment on a real shortfall, which is where a servicer wants its experienced people spending their time. At Sei we run custodial reconciliation as a desk inside the servicing system rather than a month-end batch beside it, because the same loan model the collections and escrow desks read already holds the postings, the advances, and the escrow positions the reconciliation ties out, and every break the agent finds and every remittance a human authorizes lands in the Evidence Trail where an investor audit or an agency review can replay it. The reconciliation that used to be reconstructed under an audit is the one that was already true every day.
